prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Shark attacks on humans were at the lowest levels in half a decade last year, and a Florida researcher says hard economic times may be to blame. Fewer people in the water means less chance for sharks to attack, ichthyologist George Burgess says. Sharks attacked 59 people in 2008, the lowest number of attacks since 57 in 2003, according to George Burgess, director of the International Shark Attack File, part of the Florida Museum of Natural History on the University of Florida campus in Gainesville. There were 71 attacks in 2007. "One can't help but think that the downturn in the economy played a part in it," Burgess said. Fewer people, especially outside of the United States, have the resources to go to the beach, he said. "To have a shark attack, you have to have humans and sharks in the water at the same time," Burgess said. "If you have a reduction in the number of people in the water, you're going to have a reduction in the opportunities for people and sharks to get together." "We noticed similar declines during the recession that followed the events of 2001, despite the fact that human populations continued to rise," the ichthyologist said. Sharks killed four people in 2008, Burgess said: one in California, one in Australia and two in Mexico. Forty-one of the 59 attacks worldwide came in the United States, and 32 of those occurred in Florida. Surfers accounted for 57 percent of shark attacks, swimmers and waders were the targets in 36 percent of the attacks, and divers the rest, he said. Burgess said the U.S. tends to see more attacks because of a large number of surfers, who are a favorite target of sharks. And neither the economy nor the attacks tend to keep American surfers from practicing their sport. "All they have to do is drive to the beach with the board and get into the water, and the rest is free," he said. And while an attack may make them a bit more wary, he said, "I've yet to find a surfer who says he or she won't go back into the water after a bite or a nip." When the economy improves, shark attack numbers are likely to go up again, according to Burgess, predicting the number of attacks in the next decade will surpass those of the past 10 years. "We're putting so many people in the water that humans are dictating the shark attack situation," he said.

**Shark attacks fell to five-year low in 2008, researchers say**

Shark attacks worldwide dropped to their lowest level in five years in 2008, a decline researchers say may have had less to do with sharks and more to do with people staying out of the water.

The International Shark Attack File, based at the Florida Museum of Natural History, recorded a sharp decrease in unprovoked shark attacks during the year. The drop came amid a struggling global economy, which experts said likely reduced travel, beach vacations and the amount of time people spent swimming, surfing and diving.

George Burgess, director of the International Shark Attack File, said the numbers reflect a simple reality: fewer people in the ocean means fewer chances for encounters with sharks.

“When economic conditions are difficult, people cut back on vacations and trips to the beach,” Burgess said. “If fewer people are in the water, the opportunity for shark attacks goes down.”

The decline marked the lowest total since 2003, according to the group’s annual review. Researchers emphasized that shark attack numbers often rise and fall based on human activity rather than sudden changes in shark behavior.

The United States continued to report the largest share of incidents, with Florida typically leading the nation because of its warm waters, long coastline and high number of beachgoers. Surfers and swimmers remained among the most common victims, largely because they spend extended periods in areas where sharks may be feeding or traveling.

Despite the public attention shark attacks receive, experts noted that they remain rare. Millions of people enter the ocean each year without incident, and fatal attacks make up only a small fraction of cases.

Burgess said the 2008 figures should not be interpreted as evidence that oceans are becoming safer or that shark populations are increasing or decreasing dramatically. Instead, he said, the statistics underscore the connection between human behavior and reported attacks.

“Sharks are always out there,” he said. “The variable is how many people are in their environment.”

Researchers said beachgoers can reduce their risk by swimming in groups, avoiding the water at dawn and dusk, staying away from areas where fish are schooling, and not entering the ocean with open wounds or shiny jewelry that could attract attention.

The International Shark Attack File said it will continue to monitor trends, but Burgess cautioned that future totals may rise again if the economy improves and more people return to beaches and coastal recreation.

**Shark attacks declined in 2008 as economy kept swimmers on shore, experts say**

**ATLANTA —** Reported shark attacks declined worldwide in 2008, and researchers say the drop may have had less to do with sharks than with humans.

The International Shark Attack File recorded fewer unprovoked shark attacks in 2008 than the year before, a decline ichthyologist George Burgess attributed in part to worsening economic conditions that reduced travel, beach vacations and time spent in the water.

“Shark attacks are a function of how many people are in the water,” said Burgess, longtime director of the shark attack file at the Florida Museum of Natural History. “If there are fewer people swimming, surfing and diving, there are fewer opportunities for shark-human encounters.”

The decline came during a year marked by rising unemployment, tighter household budgets and a global financial crisis that curtailed discretionary spending. Coastal tourism operators reported softer visitation in many areas, while high fuel costs earlier in the year also made long beach trips and boating outings more expensive.

Burgess said those factors matter because shark attack numbers are not simply a measure of shark behavior. They are also a reflection of human activity.

“When economic conditions are poor, people take fewer vacations, they travel shorter distances, and they may not spend as much time at the beach,” he said. “That translates into fewer people in the water.”

Florida, typically the world leader in reported shark bites, often drives the annual total because of its warm weather, long coastline and heavy concentration of surfers and swimmers. But even in places where shark populations remain stable, attack numbers can fluctuate widely depending on weather, tourism, surf conditions and holiday patterns.

Researchers caution that the year-to-year figures should not be read as evidence that oceans suddenly became safer or that sharks became less aggressive. Most shark bites are cases of mistaken identity, Burgess said, and fatal attacks remain rare.

The 2008 decline also followed years of growing coastal populations and expanding water recreation, trends that have helped push reported encounters higher over the long term. More people surf, swim, kayak and dive than in previous generations, increasing the chances that humans and sharks will cross paths.

Still, Burgess said the economic downturn offered a reminder that shark attack statistics are closely tied to human choices.

“The sharks are still out there,” he said. “What changes from year to year is how many of us are out there with them.”

“The number of shark attacks is largely a function of how many people are in the ocean,” Burgess said. “If the economy is bad and fewer people are taking vacations, surfing, diving or swimming, there are fewer opportunities for shark-human interactions.”

The United States continued to lead the world in reported shark attacks, with Florida typically accounting for the largest share because of its long coastline, warm waters and heavy beach tourism.

Researchers say most shark attacks are not fatal and often involve mistaken identity, especially in murky water or surf zones where sharks may confuse swimmers or surfers with prey. Many incidents result in minor injuries.

Burgess said the decline in 2008 should be viewed cautiously. Shark attack totals can fluctuate from year to year because of weather, ocean conditions, tourism patterns and reporting differences. A downturn in the economy, he said, may have temporarily reduced exposure by keeping would-be beachgoers closer to home.

But researchers do not expect the decrease to last indefinitely.

The number of shark attacks worldwide fell in 2008, according to findings from the International Shark Attack File, a decline researchers linked less to changes in shark behavior than to fewer people entering the water.

The file, maintained at the University of Florida, recorded a reduced number of unprovoked shark attacks compared with the previous year. Swimmers and waders also remain vulnerable, especially in nearshore areas where sharks may follow fish or patrol murky water.

Despite the overall reduction in attacks, 2008 included several fatal incidents that drew international attention. Deaths were reported in California, Australia and Mexico, underscoring that while shark attacks remain rare, they can be deadly when they occur. The California fatality was especially notable because fatal shark attacks along the U.S. West Coast are uncommon and often involve great white sharks.

Burgess and other researchers have repeatedly emphasized that shark attacks are statistically rare compared with the enormous number of people who enter the ocean each year. The International Shark Attack File tracks unprovoked attacks to better understand long-term patterns, including geography, victim activity and environmental conditions.
